Printing a multi-page plot draws the pages one after another (the script uses svg(onefile = TRUE) so that the device accepts several pages in one file).

Shingles

A shingle is lattice’s generalisation of a factor to a numeric variable: a number together with a set of possibly overlapping intervals, which are its "levels". equal.count(x, number, overlap) makes the intervals so that each contains about the same number of values, with overlap given as a fraction; shingle(x, intervals) takes the intervals you choose; as.shingle(), is.shingle(), levels() and nlevels() work as for factors. A shingle as a conditioning variable makes one panel per interval, and a row can appear in more than one panel. A numeric conditioning variable that is not a shingle is converted with shingle(), whose default intervals are the unique values, which is a panel for each distinct number and rarely what is wanted. Use equal.count() (the lattice documentation says it is often more appropriate) or cut() for a factor.

source("scenario.R")
library(lattice)

# Loan duration in days next to the pages and genre of each returned book.
books$isbn <- normalise_isbn(books$isbn)
books$genre <- factor(tolower(trimws(books$genre)))
dur <- merge(loans, books, by = "isbn")
dur$days <- as.numeric(dur$return_date - dur$loan_date)
dur <- dur[!is.na(dur$days) & dur$days >= 0, ]
svg(tempfile(fileext = ".svg"))

# A shingle is a number with overlapping intervals as its "levels".
pg <- dur$pages[!is.na(dur$pages)]
s <- equal.count(pg, number = 3, overlap = 0.1)
class(s)
#> [1] "shingle"
nlevels(s)
#> [1] 3
levels(s)
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]   84  218
#> [2,]  210  326
#> [3,]  318  436
# equal.count() asks for about the same number of values in each interval.
vapply(seq_len(nlevels(s)), \(i) {
  lim <- levels(s)[[i]]
  sum(pg >= lim[[1L]] & pg <= lim[[2L]])
}, numeric(1L))
#> [1] 19 17 16

# shingle() takes the intervals you choose.
short_long <- shingle(pg, intervals = rbind(c(0, 250), c(200, 500)))
levels(short_long)
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    0  250
#> [2,]  200  500

# Used as a condition, a shingle gives one panel per interval; rows may
# appear in more than one panel.
dur$pages_band <- equal.count(dur$pages, number = 3, overlap = 0.1)
p <- xyplot(days ~ year | pages_band, data = dur, layout = c(3, 1))
dim(p)
#> [1] 3
p$packet.sizes
#> pages_band
#>  [ 84, 218 ] [ 210, 326 ] [ 318, 436 ]
#>           19           17           16
# A numeric condition that is not a shingle is converted to one with shingle().
p_raw <- xyplot(days ~ year | pages, data = dur)
dim(p_raw)
#> [1] 13
invisible(dev.off())

Source: lattice package documentation: shingles

The three panels have 19, 17 and 16 rows, 52 in all although there are 42 loans with a known number of pages: the rows whose page count falls in an overlap are in two panels. xyplot(days ~ year | pages) made 13 panels, one for each distinct page count.

groups and keys

groups superposes subsets inside each panel and varies the graphical parameters by group, taken from the superpose.symbol and superpose.line entries of the theme. A grouping variable makes the panel function receive groups and subscripts; the default panel functions handle them, and a custom panel function must accept them or use panel.superpose(). A key (a legend) explains the groups: auto.key = TRUE draws a simple one with the levels of groups as text, auto.key = list(...) adjusts it (space is one of "top", "bottom", "left", "right", with columns, title, points, lines, rectangles, cex), key = list(...) builds one in detail, and legend = list(right = list(fun = ...)) places arbitrary grobs. With the current defaults the auto.key legend is placed on the right (the example shows names(p$legend)), and lattice 0.21 improved its default placement and its handling of the type argument.

The difference between auto.key and key is when the symbols are fixed. auto.key stores only the labels and the key is built at plotting time, so it matches the settings that are in force when the plot is drawn. key is built when the object is created, with the settings that were current then, and keeps them even if the object is printed on a device with different settings.

source("scenario.R")
library(lattice)

# Loan duration in days next to the pages and genre of each returned book.
books$isbn <- normalise_isbn(books$isbn)
books$genre <- factor(tolower(trimws(books$genre)))
dur <- merge(loans, books, by = "isbn")
dur$days <- as.numeric(dur$return_date - dur$loan_date)
dur <- dur[!is.na(dur$days) & dur$days >= 0, ]
svg(tempfile(fileext = ".svg"))
dur$kind <- factor(ifelse(dur$genre %in% c("fiction", "science fiction"),
                          "fiction", "other"))

# groups= superposes subsets in one panel, with one style per level.
p <- xyplot(days ~ pages, data = dur, groups = kind, auto.key = TRUE)
names(p$legend)
#> [1] "right"
# auto.key stores only the labels: drawSimpleKey() looks up the symbols and
# colours of the theme when the plot is drawn.
p$legend$right$fun
#> [1] "drawSimpleKey"
p$legend$right$args$text
#> [1] "fiction" "other"
levels(dur$kind)
#> [1] "fiction" "other"
p$panel.args.common$groups[1:3]
#> [1] fiction fiction fiction
#> Levels: fiction other

# A key can be placed and shaped with a list.
p2 <- xyplot(days ~ pages, data = dur, groups = kind,
             auto.key = list(space = "top", title = "Kind", columns = 2))
names(p2$legend)
#> [1] "top"

# key= is fixed when the object is made; auto.key adapts when it is drawn.
p3 <- xyplot(days ~ pages, data = dur, groups = kind,
             key = simpleKey(levels(dur$kind), points = TRUE))
names(p3$legend)
#> [1] "top"
p3$legend$top$fun
#> [1] "draw.key"
names(p3$legend$top$args$key)
#> [1] "text"       "col"        "cex"        "alpha"      "font"
#> [6] "fontface"   "fontfamily" "points"

# Without groups there is nothing to key, so auto.key adds no legend.
p4 <- xyplot(days ~ pages, data = dur, auto.key = TRUE)
length(p4$legend)
#> [1] 0

# subscripts= are the row numbers of each panel's rows in the data.
p5 <- xyplot(days ~ pages | kind, data = dur, subscripts = TRUE)
p5$panel.args[[1L]]$subscripts[1:5]
#> [1] 1 2 3 4 5
invisible(dev.off())

Source: lattice package documentation: xyplot

Panel functions

The panel function is where the drawing happens. A panel function receives the x and y of one packet and every argument of the high-level call that lattice did not use itself, so pch = 16 given to xyplot() arrives in the panel function. The panel function must be written with grid, not with base graphics: lines() and points() do not work inside a panel (the error is "plot.new has not been called yet"), and lattice supplies grid versions that behave like them, named panel.* and l*: panel.points()/lpoints(), panel.lines()/llines(), panel.text()/ltext(), panel.segments(), panel.rect(), panel.polygon() and so on.

The building blocks in ?panel.functions are the usual ones:

Function What it draws

panel.xyplot(x, y, type, groups, smooth, grid, ...)

The default panel function of xyplot().

panel.abline(a, b, h, v, reg) and panel.refline()

Lines: a slope and intercept, a horizontal or vertical line, or a fitted model (panel.refline() draws a reference line in the reference style of the theme).

panel.lmline(x, y), panel.loess(x, y), panel.spline(x, y), panel.average(x, y, fun)

Smoothers and summaries added on top of the points.

panel.grid(h, v)

A background grid; positive h and v are the number of lines, and -1 places them at pretty locations, which usually match the axis labels.

panel.rug(x, y), panel.curve(expr), panel.fill(col), panel.mathdensity()

A rug, a curve from an expression, a background fill, and a theoretical density.

panel.superpose(x, y, groups, subscripts, panel.groups)

Calls panel.groups once per group.

panel.number(), packet.number(), current.row(), current.column(), which.packet()

Where in the array the current panel is (below).

Source: lattice package documentation: panel.functions

Two numbers say which panel is being drawn. panel.number() is the order of drawing, 1, 2, 3, …​, and packet.number() the position of the packet in the natural order of the conditioning levels. They coincide unless perm.cond or index.cond changes the order, which is what the second half of the example shows. They are available inside the panel function, the strip function and the axis function, and while interacting with a plot through trellis.focus(), but not in the prepanel function, which runs before the plotting.

The panel function is evaluated when the plot is printed, not when xyplot() is called. The script records what each panel receives in an environment, and the count is zero until print(). Note ... in the panel function: it passes pch = 16 on to panel.xyplot().

source("scenario.R")
library(lattice)

# Loan duration in days next to the pages and genre of each returned book.
books$isbn <- normalise_isbn(books$isbn)
books$genre <- factor(tolower(trimws(books$genre)))
dur <- merge(loans, books, by = "isbn")
dur$days <- as.numeric(dur$return_date - dur$loan_date)
dur <- dur[!is.na(dur$days) & dur$days >= 0, ]
svg(tempfile(fileext = ".svg"))
seen <- new.env()

# A panel function gets the x and y of one packet plus everything else that
# the high-level call did not use. Keep `...` so those extras flow through.
loan_panel <- \(x, y, ...) {
  panel.grid(h = -1, v = -1, col = "grey85")
  panel.xyplot(x, y, ...)
  ok <- !is.na(x) & !is.na(y)
  if (sum(ok) > 2L) {
    panel.lmline(x[ok], y[ok], col = "firebrick")
  }
  panel.text(min(x, na.rm = TRUE), max(y, na.rm = TRUE),
             labels = panel.number(), adj = c(0, 1))
  assign(
    sprintf("panel_%d", panel.number()),
    c(packet = packet.number(), n = length(x)),
    envir = seen
  )
}

p <- xyplot(days ~ pages | genre, data = dur, panel = loan_panel, pch = 16)
# xyplot() has not called the panel function: that happens when it is drawn.
length(ls(seen))
#> [1] 0
print(p)
length(ls(seen))
#> [1] 6
mget(c("panel_1", "panel_2", "panel_6"), envir = seen)
#> $panel_1
#> packet      n
#>      1      5
#>
#> $panel_2
#> packet      n
#>      2     18
#>
#> $panel_6
#> packet      n
#>      6     13
#>

# panel.number counts the panels in drawing order; packet.number is the
# position of the packet in the natural order of the conditioning levels.
# They differ once the order is changed.
rev_p <- update(p, index.cond = list(6:1))
rm(list = ls(seen), envir = seen)
print(rev_p)
vapply(mget(sprintf("panel_%d", 1:3), envir = seen), \(v) v[["packet"]],
       numeric(1L))
#> panel_1 panel_2 panel_3
#>       6       5       4
invisible(dev.off())

Source: lattice package documentation: panel.number

Because the panel function runs when the plot is printed, anything it reads from the global environment is read then, not when the object was made. The script lets the panel function write to an environment it was given rather than using <<-. Also remember that x and y can contain NA: lattice passes the packet to a custom panel function as it is (the first panel of the example has missing page counts), so the line-fitting call above checks ok first.

Scales

scales is a list that controls the axes: tick marks, labels, limits, and whether the limits are shared. It can hold the same components for both axes or a sub-list for x and y, and a bare character string is read as relation.

Component Effect

relation

"same" (the default: all panels share the limits), "free" (each panel gets its own) or "sliced" (own limits, but the same length of range, so slopes are comparable).

log

TRUE (base 10), a number or "e": the variable is log-transformed before it reaches the panel function, and the ticks are labelled in the original scale.

at, labels, tick.number

Positions and labels of ticks, or the suggested number of ticks.

limits

As xlim and ylim.

draw, alternating

Whether to draw the axis at all, and whether the labels alternate between the two sides of the array (default), or a vector choosing for each row or column: 0 none, 1 bottom or left, 2 top or right, 3 both.

rot, cex, col, font, tck

Appearance of tick labels and marks.

abbreviate, minlength

Abbreviate long labels, as in scales = list(x = list(abbreviate = TRUE)).

equispaced.log

Equally spaced ticks for log scales (default) or ticks as in traditional graphics.

Source: lattice package documentation: xyplot

With relation = "same", x.limits holds one pair; with "free" or "sliced" it holds a list with one pair per panel, which the script prints.

source("scenario.R")
library(lattice)

# Loan duration in days next to the pages and genre of each returned book.
books$isbn <- normalise_isbn(books$isbn)
books$genre <- factor(tolower(trimws(books$genre)))
dur <- merge(loans, books, by = "isbn")
dur$days <- as.numeric(dur$return_date - dur$loan_date)
dur <- dur[!is.na(dur$days) & dur$days >= 0, ]
svg(tempfile(fileext = ".svg"))
n3 <- dur[dur$genre %in% c("fiction", "science fiction", "poetry"), ]
n3$genre <- droplevels(n3$genre)

# relation = "same" (the default) gives every panel the same limits.
same <- xyplot(days ~ pages | genre, data = n3, layout = c(3, 1))
same$x.limits
#> [1]  65.46 432.54
same$y.limits
#> [1] -1.52 39.52

# relation = "free" works the limits out panel by panel: a list, not a pair.
free <- update(same, scales = list(relation = "free"))
class(free$x.limits)
#> [1] "list"
length(free$x.limits)
#> [1] 3
free$x.limits[[3L]]
#> [1] 315.84 416.16

# "sliced" keeps the length of the range the same but moves it.
sliced <- update(same, scales = list(y = list(relation = "sliced")))
vapply(sliced$y.limits, diff, numeric(1L))
#> [1] 41.04 41.04 41.04

# log = TRUE log-transforms the data; the tick labels show the original scale.
logx <- xyplot(days ~ pages | genre, data = n3, layout = c(3, 1),
               scales = list(x = list(log = TRUE)))
logx$x.limits
#> [1] 1.897702 2.659565
logx$x.scales$log
#> [1] TRUE
logx$panel.args[[1L]]$x[1:3]
#> [1] 2.330414 2.330414 2.330414
# The log scale is part of how the packets are built: update() refuses it.
tryCatch(update(same, scales = list(x = list(log = TRUE))),
         warning = \(w) conditionMessage(w))
#> [1] "log scales cannot be changed via 'update'"

# Explicit limits, tick positions and labels.
fixed <- update(same, xlim = c(0, 500),
                scales = list(x = list(at = c(0, 250, 500),
                                       labels = c("0", "250", "500"))))
fixed$x.limits
#> [1]   0 500
fixed$x.scales$at
#> [1]   0 250 500
invisible(dev.off())

Source: lattice package documentation: xyplot

The warning "log scales cannot be changed via 'update'" is real and instructive: a log scale transforms the data when the packets are built, so it cannot be applied to an existing object, and update(p, scales = list(x = list(log = TRUE))) warns and leaves the scale unchanged. The help page of xyplot() says that scales = list(x = list(log = 2)) is equivalent to writing log2(x) in the formula, apart from the axis labelling. More generally the help page of update.trellis() says that anything that would change the data within each panel (formula, data, groups, subscripts, subset) is not available to update().

Strips and titles

The strips above the panels show the conditioning level. strip = FALSE removes them, strip = strip.custom(...) changes them (strip.names = TRUE shows the variable name with the level, strip.levels = c(TRUE, FALSE) controls whether levels are shown, style changes the look, bg and fg the colours), strip.left = TRUE puts strips on the left of the panels, which suits wide, short panels, and par.strip.text = list(cex, col, font, lines, abbreviate, minlength) formats the text. The title and labels are main, sub, xlab, ylab, and xlab.top and ylab.right for the other sides; each can be a character string, an expression (plotmath), a list that passes arguments such as cex, col and font to the text grob, or a grob. xlab = NULL removes a label.

source("scenario.R")
library(lattice)

# Loan duration in days next to the pages and genre of each returned book.
books$isbn <- normalise_isbn(books$isbn)
books$genre <- factor(tolower(trimws(books$genre)))
dur <- merge(loans, books, by = "isbn")
dur$days <- as.numeric(dur$return_date - dur$loan_date)
dur <- dur[!is.na(dur$days) & dur$days >= 0, ]
svg(tempfile(fileext = ".svg"))

# Strips label the panels; strip.custom() changes how they are drawn.
p <- xyplot(days ~ pages | genre, data = dur)
class(p$strip)
#> [1] "character"
class(update(p, strip = FALSE)$strip)
#> [1] "logical"
named <- update(
  p, strip = strip.custom(strip.names = TRUE, strip.levels = TRUE)
)
class(named$strip)
#> [1] "function"

# par.strip.text controls the text of the strips: size, colour and height.
tall <- update(p, par.strip.text = list(cex = 0.8, lines = 2))
tall$par.strip.text
#> $cex
#> [1] 0.8
#>
#> $lines
#> [1] 2
#>

# Long labels can be abbreviated rather than wrapped.
abbr <- update(p, par.strip.text = list(abbreviate = TRUE, minlength = 4))
abbr$par.strip.text
#> $abbreviate
#> [1] TRUE
#>
#> $minlength
#> [1] 4
#>
# Strips can sit on the left of each panel.
left <- update(p, strip = FALSE, strip.left = TRUE)
class(left$strip.left)
#> [1] "function"
print(abbr)
invisible(dev.off())

Source: lattice package documentation: strip.default

Themes and par.settings

Lattice does not read par(). Its graphical parameters are in a settings list per device, queried with trellis.par.get(), changed with trellis.par.set(), and set for one object with the par.settings argument. A change to par(mfrow = ...) or par(mar = ...) has no effect on lattice plots (the lattice help page says so, and the base-versus-grid script above proves it for the panel width). Grid parameters that apply to the whole plot go in the grid.pars component of the settings.

The settings are kept per device name, not per device instance. Opening a second svg() device inherits what the first one left behind, and trellis.device() resets them: the example shows the symbol colour changed, then inherited by the next svg() device, then reset by trellis.device(). The help page says the settings of a device name are created when trellis.device() opens it or when a lattice plot is first drawn on it. A change with trellis.par.set() therefore lasts for the session unless the device is reopened with trellis.device(), and par.settings is the way to change only one plot.

source("scenario.R")
library(lattice)

# Loan duration in days next to the pages and genre of each returned book.
books$isbn <- normalise_isbn(books$isbn)
books$genre <- factor(tolower(trimws(books$genre)))
dur <- merge(loans, books, by = "isbn")
dur$days <- as.numeric(dur$return_date - dur$loan_date)
dur <- dur[!is.na(dur$days) & dur$days >= 0, ]
svg(tempfile(fileext = ".svg"))

# The settings belong to the current device; the first plot creates them.
settings <- trellis.par.get()
class(settings)
#> [1] "list"
length(settings)
#> [1] 36
head(names(settings), 8L)
#> [1] "grid.pars"        "fontsize"         "background"       "panel.background"
#> [5] "clip"             "add.line"         "add.text"         "plot.polygon"
settings$plot.symbol
#> $alpha
#> [1] 1
#>
#> $cex
#> [1] 0.8
#>
#> $col
#> [1] "#0072B2"
#>
#> $font
#> [1] 1
#>
#> $pch
#> [1] 1
#>
#> $fill
#> [1] "transparent"
#>
trellis.par.get("add.line")$col
#> [1] "black"

# trellis.par.set() changes the settings of the open device, until it closes.
trellis.par.set("plot.symbol", list(col = "firebrick", pch = 16))
trellis.par.get("plot.symbol")$col
#> [1] "firebrick"
trellis.par.set(list(add.line = list(col = "grey40", lwd = 2)))
trellis.par.get("add.line")$lwd
#> [1] 2

# par.settings= travels with one object and does not touch the device.
trellis.par.set("plot.symbol", list(col = "black", pch = 1))
blue <- list(plot.symbol = list(col = "steelblue", pch = 19))
p <- xyplot(days ~ pages, data = dur, par.settings = blue)
p$par.settings$plot.symbol$col
#> [1] "steelblue"
trellis.par.get("plot.symbol")$col
#> [1] "black"

# simpleTheme() builds the common case: symbols, lines and fill in one call.
th <- simpleTheme(col = c("steelblue", "tomato"), pch = 16)
names(th)
#> [1] "plot.symbol"       "plot.line"         "plot.polygon"
#> [4] "superpose.symbol"  "superpose.line"    "superpose.polygon"
th$superpose.symbol$col
#> [1] "steelblue" "tomato"
invisible(dev.off())

# The settings are kept per device *name*, so a second svg() device inherits
# what the first one left behind ...
svg(tempfile(fileext = ".svg"))
trellis.par.get("plot.symbol")$col
#> [1] "black"
invisible(dev.off())
# ... until trellis.device() opens it and resets the settings to the defaults.
trellis.device(svg, file = tempfile(fileext = ".svg"))
trellis.par.get("plot.symbol")$col
#> [1] "#0072B2"
invisible(dev.off())

Source: lattice package documentation: trellis.par.get

simpleTheme(col, pch, ...) builds the common change (symbols, lines and fill colours) as a theme list. A full theme is made by standard.theme(), custom_theme() and classic.theme().

The default colours changed in R 4.3.0

Older tutorials show lattice plots in a recognisable blue and magenta. The help page of standard.theme() says that since R 4.3.0 a new set of defaults, based on HCL palettes, is used, and the NEWS of lattice 0.21 records the change to modern palettes. The default symbol colour is now #0072B2 and the superposed groups use the Okabe-Ito palette; the earlier look is classic.theme("pdf"), which can be set for the session with lattice.options(default.theme = classic.theme("pdf")) in a startup script, or for one plot with par.settings.

library(lattice)

# The default colours come from an HCL palette; classic.theme() restores the
# colours that older tutorials show.
modern <- standard.theme()
classic <- classic.theme("pdf")
modern$plot.symbol$col
#> [1] "#0072B2"
classic$plot.symbol$col
#> [1] "#0080ff"
modern$superpose.symbol$col[1:3]
#> [1] "#0072B2" "#E69F00" "#009E73"
classic$superpose.symbol$col[1:3]
#> [1] "#0080ff"   "#ff00ff"   "darkgreen"

# A theme is a list that trellis.par.set() or par.settings= accepts.
class(modern)
#> [1] "list"
c("plot.symbol", "superpose.line", "strip.background") %in% names(modern)
#> [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE

# The old look in one object, without changing the session.
svg(tempfile(fileext = ".svg"))
p <- xyplot(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars, par.settings = classic.theme("pdf"))
p$par.settings$plot.symbol$col
#> [1] "#0080ff"
invisible(dev.off())

Source: lattice package documentation: standard.theme

Several plots on one page

print(x, split = c(col, row, ncol, nrow), position = c(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax), more = FALSE, newpage = TRUE) places a trellis plot on a page that holds others. split says that the plot goes in cell (col, row) of an ncol by nrow array, with the origin at the top left. position places it in a rectangle with coordinates from 0 to 1 and the origin at the bottom left, and the two can be combined. more = TRUE says the page is not finished, so the next plot is drawn on the same page instead of starting a new one. newpage = FALSE draws into the current grid viewport, which makes it possible to embed a lattice plot in an arbitrary viewport, and draw.in = "name" goes to a named viewport. The prefix argument names the plot’s viewports and grobs; by default it is plot_01, plot_02, and so on, by serial number on the current page. This replaces gridExtra::grid.arrange() (not installed here) for lattice plots, and par(mfrow) and layout() of base graphics, which do not work. The help page warns that positioning a multi-page display does not work.

source("scenario.R")
library(lattice)

# Loan duration in days next to the pages and genre of each returned book.
books$isbn <- normalise_isbn(books$isbn)
books$genre <- factor(tolower(trimws(books$genre)))
dur <- merge(loans, books, by = "isbn")
dur$days <- as.numeric(dur$return_date - dur$loan_date)
dur <- dur[!is.na(dur$days) & dur$days >= 0, ]
library(grid)
svg(tempfile(fileext = ".svg"))

scatter <- xyplot(days ~ pages, data = dur, main = "Duration by length")
boxes <- bwplot(genre ~ days, data = dur, main = "Duration by genre")

# split = c(x, y, nx, ny): the plot goes in cell (x, y) of an nx by ny array;
# more = TRUE says the page is not finished.
print(scatter, split = c(1, 1, 2, 1), more = TRUE)
print(boxes, split = c(2, 1, 2, 1))

# Each plot got its own prefix in the names of its viewports.
vps <- grid.ls(viewports = TRUE, grobs = FALSE, print = FALSE)$name
unique(sub("\\..*$", "", grep("toplevel", vps, value = TRUE)))
#> [1] "plot_01" "plot_02"

# position = c(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) places the plot in a rectangle of the
# page, in [0, 1] coordinates, and can overlap another plot.
grid.newpage()
print(scatter, position = c(0, 0, 1, 1), more = TRUE)
print(update(boxes, main = NULL), position = c(0.55, 0.5, 0.98, 0.95))
vps <- grid.ls(viewports = TRUE, grobs = FALSE, print = FALSE)$name
unique(sub("\\..*$", "", grep("toplevel", vps, value = TRUE)))
#> [1] "plot_01" "plot_02"

# newpage = FALSE draws into the current grid viewport instead.
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(width = 0.5, height = 0.5, name = "inset"))
print(scatter, newpage = FALSE)
current.vpPath()
#> inset
popViewport()

# An explicit prefix makes the viewport names predictable.
print(scatter, newpage = TRUE, prefix = "loans")
trellis.vpname("panel", column = 1, row = 1, prefix = "loans")
#> [1] "loans.panel.1.1.vp"
invisible(dev.off())

Source: lattice package documentation: print.trellis

update(), trellis.last.object() and the plot arguments

update(p, ...) returns a copy of a trellis object with the named components replaced, using the same names as the high-level call; it records the change in the call component. The help page says that perm.cond and index.cond change the arrangement without recalculating the data subsets. A component set to NULL is removed. Some changes cannot be made this way: the data cannot change, and neither can the log scale above. t() transposes a plot with two conditioning variables. trellis.last.object() returns the last object that was printed (lattice saves it on printing, which the save.object option controls), and trellis.last.object(...) is update() on it. The plot.args component holds arguments for print() that travel with the object, such as a split.

source("scenario.R")
library(lattice)

# Loan duration in days next to the pages and genre of each returned book.
books$isbn <- normalise_isbn(books$isbn)
books$genre <- factor(tolower(trimws(books$genre)))
dur <- merge(loans, books, by = "isbn")
dur$days <- as.numeric(dur$return_date - dur$loan_date)
dur <- dur[!is.na(dur$days) & dur$days >= 0, ]
svg(tempfile(fileext = ".svg"))
base <- xyplot(days ~ pages | genre, data = dur, layout = c(3, 2))

# update() returns a modified copy; the original object does not change.
titled <- update(base, main = "Loan duration by length", xlab = "Pages",
                 ylab = "Days", type = c("p", "r"))
base$main
#> NULL
titled$main
#> [1] "Loan duration by length"
base$call
#> xyplot(days ~ pages | genre, data = dur, layout = c(3, 2))
titled$call
#> xyplot(days ~ pages | genre, data = dur, layout = c(3, 2), main = "Loan duration by length",
#>     xlab = "Pages", ylab = "Days", type = c("p", "r"))
identical(base$layout, titled$layout)
#> [1] TRUE

# Components that are not named stay as they were. NULL removes one.
untitled <- update(titled, main = NULL)
is.null(untitled$main)
#> [1] TRUE

# update() of a plot that was drawn without being saved: the last one drawn.
print(base)
last <- trellis.last.object()
class(last)
#> [1] "trellis"
last$call
#> xyplot(days ~ pages | genre, data = dur, layout = c(3, 2))
trellis.last.object(xlab = "Pages in the book")$xlab
#> [1] "Pages in the book"
invisible(dev.off())

Source: lattice package documentation: update.trellis

Lattice is grid: trellis.focus()

Because a lattice plot is a tree of grid viewports and grobs, it can be changed after it is drawn. The names are predictable: for the plot with prefix plot_01, the panel in column 2 and row 1 is the viewport plot_01.panel.2.1.vp, its strip is plot_01.strip.2.1.vp, and trellis.vpname() builds the names. trellis.focus(name, column, row) makes the viewport current, so that any grid function can draw in it, and trellis.unfocus() returns to the top. Rows count from the bottom unless the plot was made with as.table = TRUE. The help page calls these interaction functions experimental, so their details may change. trellis.panelArgs() returns the data of the focused panel, current.panel.limits() its data limits, and panel.identify() and trellis.grobname() are the tools for interactive use. The lattice-aware panel functions (panel.abline(), panel.text()) draw into the focused panel, and what they draw is a named grob, so it can also be found with grid.ls().

source("scenario.R")
library(lattice)

# Loan duration in days next to the pages and genre of each returned book.
books$isbn <- normalise_isbn(books$isbn)
books$genre <- factor(tolower(trimws(books$genre)))
dur <- merge(loans, books, by = "isbn")
dur$days <- as.numeric(dur$return_date - dur$loan_date)
dur <- dur[!is.na(dur$days) & dur$days >= 0, ]
library(grid)
svg(tempfile(fileext = ".svg"))
print(xyplot(days ~ pages | genre, data = dur, layout = c(3, 2)))

# Every panel is a grid viewport with a predictable name.
trellis.vpname("panel", column = 2, row = 1)
#> [1] "plot_01.panel.2.1.vp"
trellis.vpname("strip", column = 2, row = 1)
#> [1] "plot_01.strip.2.1.vp"

# trellis.focus() makes a panel the current viewport, so grid code can draw.
trellis.focus("panel", column = 2, row = 1)
current.vpPath()
#> plot_01.toplevel.vp::plot_01.panel.2.1.vp
lim <- current.panel.limits()
lim$xlim
#> [1]  63.92 456.08
lim$ylim
#> [1] -1.52 39.52
# The data of the focused panel is available as it was passed to the panel.
args <- trellis.panelArgs()
length(args$x)
#> [1] 18
panel.abline(h = loan_days, lty = "dashed", col = "grey40")
panel.number()
#> [1] 2
trellis.unfocus()
current.vpPath()
#> NULL

# The abline is now an object on the page, and the page is a big tree: this
# six-panel plot has one entry for every viewport it pushed.
length(grid.ls(viewports = TRUE, grobs = FALSE, print = FALSE)$name)
#> [1] 122
grep("abline", grid.ls(print = FALSE)$name, value = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE)
#> [1] "plot_01.abline.h.panel.2.1"
invisible(dev.off())

Source: lattice package documentation: interaction

The lattice package ships one vignette, vignette("grid", package = "lattice"), about using raw grid code with lattice (added in lattice 0.21; lattice package documentation: the grid vignette). The help page of print.trellis() says that the grid display tree is kept after the plot is produced, which older versions of lattice and grid did not do. The tree can be listed with grid.ls(viewports = TRUE), and it is long: the six-panel plot of the script has 122 entries after the focus step (viewports for each panel and strip and their "off" counterparts), which is why a script that wants to test something looks up a name rather than printing the listing.

Options, devices and a lattice-wide default

lattice.options() holds the package-wide non-graphical settings; lattice.getOption(name) reads one. The ones used most are default.args (the defaults of as.table, aspect, auto.key, between, grid, skip, strip and the scale and axis functions, as the script lists), default.theme, save.object, panel.error, drop.unused.levels and the names of the default panel functions (panel.xyplot, panel.bwplot, and so on). lattice.options(old) restores the value returned by a previous call. A call-specific change is the lattice.options = argument of a high-level function, which applies only for that call and stays with the object.

trellis.device(device, color, theme, new, retain, ...) opens a device and initialises the lattice settings for it, with theme a list, a function that returns one, or its name. It is not needed to draw a lattice plot, since any open device works and the first plot creates the settings for it. Older tutorials call trellis.device() and trellis.par.set() at the top of every script to get a white background and a good colour scheme; with the current defaults that is rarely needed. The script shows the call with svg and col.whitebg(), the older theme that sets a transparent background.

source("scenario.R")
library(lattice)

# Loan duration in days next to the pages and genre of each returned book.
books$isbn <- normalise_isbn(books$isbn)
books$genre <- factor(tolower(trimws(books$genre)))
dur <- merge(loans, books, by = "isbn")
dur$days <- as.numeric(dur$return_date - dur$loan_date)
dur <- dur[!is.na(dur$days) & dur$days >= 0, ]
svg(tempfile(fileext = ".svg"))

# Package-wide options that are not graphical parameters.
opts <- lattice.options()
length(opts) > 20
#> [1] TRUE
head(sort(names(opts)), 6L)
#> [1] "axis.padding"       "axis.units"         "banking"
#> [4] "default.args"       "drop.unused.levels" "highlight.gpar"
names(lattice.getOption("default.args"))
#>  [1] "as.table"          "aspect"            "auto.key"
#>  [4] "between"           "grid"              "skip"
#>  [7] "strip"             "xscale.components" "yscale.components"
#> [10] "axis"
lattice.getOption("default.args")$as.table
#> [1] FALSE
lattice.getOption("save.object")
#> [1] TRUE

# Change one for the whole session ... and put it back.
old <- lattice.options(default.args = list(as.table = TRUE, aspect = "fill"))
xyplot(days ~ pages | genre, data = dur)$as.table
#> [1] TRUE
lattice.options(old)
xyplot(days ~ pages | genre, data = dur)$as.table
#> [1] FALSE

# lattice.options= on one call is temporary and stays with that object.
p <- xyplot(days ~ pages | genre, data = dur,
            lattice.options = list(default.args = list(as.table = TRUE)))
p$lattice.options$default.args
#> $as.table
#> [1] TRUE
#>
invisible(dev.off())

# trellis.device() opens a device and initialises the lattice settings; its
# first argument is a device function or its name.
trellis.device(svg, file = tempfile(fileext = ".svg"), theme = "col.whitebg")
dev.cur()
#> svg
#>   2
trellis.par.get("background")$col
#> [1] "transparent"
invisible(dev.off())

Source: lattice package documentation: lattice.options

Other packages

The add-on package latticeExtra (not installed here) is the extension package the lattice help page itself points to; it adds, among other things, xscale.components.logpower for log axes, and it is named here and not used. gridExtra (also not installed) provides grid.arrange() and table grobs; for lattice plots print(split =) does the same job.

Grid underneath ggplot2

ggplot2 draws with grid too, in its own way: a plot is built from layers, and ggplotGrob() turns it into a gtable, a gTree that is a table of grobs (a layout whose cells hold the panel, the axes, the strips and the legend). So grid knowledge applies to ggplot2 (editing a drawn ggplot2 figure, putting it in a viewport, drawing annotations with grid functions), and lattice and ggplot2 plots can sit on the same page. The class vector of the plot in the script shows the S7 object system that ggplot2 4.0 adopted (the ggplot2 NEWS says the S3 parts were replaced with S7 ones; see The S7 Object System).

source("scenario.R")
library(lattice)

# Loan duration in days next to the pages and genre of each returned book.
books$isbn <- normalise_isbn(books$isbn)
books$genre <- factor(tolower(trimws(books$genre)))
dur <- merge(loans, books, by = "isbn")
dur$days <- as.numeric(dur$return_date - dur$loan_date)
dur <- dur[!is.na(dur$days) & dur$days >= 0, ]
library(ggplot2)
library(grid)
svg(tempfile(fileext = ".svg"))

# ggplot2 builds its plot out of grid objects: ggplotGrob() returns the gtable.
paged <- dur[!is.na(dur$pages), ]
gg <- ggplot(paged, aes(pages, days)) +
  geom_point()
class(gg)
#> [1] "ggplot2::ggplot" "ggplot"          "ggplot2::gg"     "S7_object"
#> [5] "gg"
g <- ggplotGrob(gg)
class(g)
#> [1] "gtable" "gTree"  "grob"   "gDesc"
is.grob(g)
#> [1] TRUE
head(g$layout$name, 6L)
#> [1] "background" "spacer"     "axis-l"     "spacer"     "axis-t"
#> [6] "panel"
# The panel itself is a gTree of grobs.
panel <- g$grobs[[which(g$layout$name == "panel")]]
class(panel)
#> [1] "gTree" "grob"  "gDesc"
any(grepl("geom_point", childNames(panel), fixed = TRUE))
#> [1] TRUE
# Both systems end up as grobs on the same page.
print(gg)
grid.ls(print = FALSE)$name[1L]
#> [1] "layout"
invisible(dev.off())

Source: ggplot2 package documentation: ggplotGrob

Source: lattice package documentation: Lattice

The choice is partly taste and partly the data. lattice is small, ships with R, and is at its best for many comparable panels of the same display with scales shared on purpose, which was its design; ggplot2 is better when a plot is made of layers of different geometry and when the style should be consistent across a project. Both are worth reading the data from the same data frame, and neither replaces base graphics for a quick look.

Pitfalls

  • No print() where R does not print. A lattice or ggplot2 object returned from a function or created in a loop is not drawn (R FAQ 7.22); return it and print it at the top level, or call print().

  • Base graphics functions in a panel function. lines(), points(), abline() and text() fail inside a panel with "plot.new has not been called yet". Use panel.lines()/llines(), panel.points(), panel.abline() and panel.text(). By default lattice catches the error and writes it in the panel (panel.error), so a failed panel shows as text and the script continues; use print(p, panel.error = stop) while developing.

  • A panel function without .... The extra arguments of the high-level call, such as pch = 16, are dropped silently, with no message. Always end a custom panel function’s arguments with ... and pass it on.

  • Numeric conditioning variables. xyplot(y ~ x | z) with a numeric z makes one panel per distinct value. Use equal.count(z, number = 4) or cut(z, ...).

  • Mixing systems. par() has no effect on grid or lattice; layout() and grid.layout() are different functions, and base functions and grid functions do not know each other’s state. To combine, use print(split =) for lattice plots, a grid layout of viewports, or gridBase/gridGraphics.

  • update() cannot change data. formula, data, groups, subscripts and subset are not accepted by update(), and a log scale cannot be added (a warning says so). Build a new plot instead.

  • The settings belong to the device name. A trellis.par.set() made for one svg() device is still there on the next one in the same session. Use par.settings for a change that is meant for one plot, and trellis.device() to reset.

  • dimnames() is not what is shown. After [ or index.cond, dim() is right and dimnames() still lists every level.

  • Panel order. With as.table = FALSE (the default) panels start at the bottom left, like a graph, which is the reverse of reading order; as.table = TRUE starts at the top left.

  • Grob names and counters. Automatically generated grob names depend on a counter (GRID.rect.1), and a figure that is drawn more than once in a session gets different numbers. Name grobs that code will look for.

  • Interactive state. grid.locator(), panel.identify() and trellis.focus() called without a panel read the mouse, so they need an interactive screen device; they are not run on this page.

  • The Rplots.pdf file. A drawing call with no open device opens the default one; under Rscript that writes Rplots.pdf in the working directory. Open a device first (png(), svg(), pdf(NULL)) and close it with dev.off().

source("scenario.R")
library(lattice)

# Loan duration in days next to the pages and genre of each returned book.
books$isbn <- normalise_isbn(books$isbn)
books$genre <- factor(tolower(trimws(books$genre)))
dur <- merge(loans, books, by = "isbn")
dur$days <- as.numeric(dur$return_date - dur$loan_date)
dur <- dur[!is.na(dur$days) & dur$days >= 0, ]
svg(tempfile(fileext = ".svg"))
msg <- \(expr) {
  tryCatch(
    expr,
    error = \(e) conditionMessage(e),
    warning = \(w) conditionMessage(w)
  )
}

# A variable that is not in `data` or the formula's environment.
msg(xyplot(days ~ no_such_column | genre, data = dur))
#> [1] "object 'no_such_column' not found"
# A data frame is needed when the formula uses column names.
msg(xyplot(days ~ pages | genre))
#> [1] "object 'genre' not found"
# A conditioning variable that is a number becomes a shingle: one panel for
# each distinct value, which is rarely what was meant.
dim(xyplot(days ~ year | pages, data = dur))
#> [1] 13

# An error in a panel function does not stop printing: the message is drawn
# inside the panel and print() returns normally.
failing <- \(x, y, ...) stop("no data for this packet")
p <- xyplot(days ~ pages | genre, data = dur, panel = failing)
class(print(p))
#> [1] "trellis"
# panel.error = stop raises it instead.
msg(print(p, panel.error = stop))
#> [1] "no data for this packet"

# A panel function without `...` silently ignores extra arguments.
no_dots <- \(x, y) panel.xyplot(x, y)
p2 <- xyplot(days ~ pages, data = dur, panel = no_dots, pch = 16, col = "red")
class(print(p2, panel.error = stop))
#> [1] "trellis"

# Base graphics functions do not work inside a lattice panel.
base_in_panel <- \(x, y, ...) lines(x, y)
p3 <- xyplot(days ~ pages, data = dur, panel = base_in_panel)
msg(print(p3, panel.error = stop))
#> [1] "plot.new has not been called yet"

# A factor on the response is allowed in xyplot: the levels label the axis.
yf <- xyplot(genre ~ days, data = dur)
class(yf$y.limits)
#> [1] "character"
invisible(dev.off())

Source: lattice package documentation: print.trellis

The output shows each case. The missing column and the missing data are ordinary object-not-found errors from evaluating the formula. A panel function that fails does not stop print() (the class of the result is still "trellis") unless panel.error = stop is passed, and then the message is the one the panel function raised. An extra argument given to a panel function that lacks ... produces no message. A base graphics call inside a panel gives "plot.new has not been called yet". And xyplot() accepts a factor as the response and labels the axis with its levels.

Names from old tutorials that were removed from grid and lattice still exist as stubs, so that the error names the replacement. The script calls four grid names and lattice’s parallel(); grid.prompt(), removed in R 3.0.0, no longer exists at all, and the script checks that.

library(grid)
svg(tempfile(fileext = ".svg"))
msg <- \(expr) {
  tryCatch(expr, error = \(e) conditionMessage(e))
}

# These names from old tutorials still exist, but only to say they are gone.
msg(push.viewport(viewport()))
#> [1] "'push.viewport' is defunct.\nUse 'pushViewport' instead.\nSee help(\"Defunct\")"
msg(grid.convertWidth(unit(1, "inches"), "cm"))
#> [1] "'grid.convertWidth' is defunct.\nUse 'convertWidth' instead.\nSee help(\"Defunct\")"
msg(grid.collection())
#> [1] "'grid.collection' is defunct.\nUse 'gTree' instead.\nSee help(\"Defunct\")"
msg(convertNative(unit(1, "native")))
#> [1] "'convertNative' is defunct.\nUse 'convertUnit' instead.\nSee help(\"Defunct\")"
# grid.prompt() was removed in R 3.0.0; the replacement is a base function.
exists("grid.prompt", envir = asNamespace("grid"))
#> [1] FALSE
is.function(devAskNewPage)
#> [1] TRUE
# lattice's parallel() is the same kind of stub since lattice 0.22.
msg(lattice::parallel(~ mtcars[1:3]))
#> [1] "'parallel' is defunct.\nUse 'parallelplot' instead.\nSee help(\"Defunct\")"
invisible(dev.off())

Source: R documentation: grid-defunct

Version notes

The grid model itself has changed little; the notable changes are additions to the graphics engine and to lattice’s defaults. The entries come from the NEWS files (R NEWS, R 3.x NEWS) and the NEWS of lattice, which is shipped with the package (NEWS.md) and published on CRAN.

Version Change

R 3.0.0

grid.prompt() removed: use devAskNewPage().

R 4.0.0

New internal implementation of grid units (a different print format for unit arithmetic, faster operations, new unitType() and unit.psum()).

R 4.1.0

Gradient and pattern fills (gpar(fill = linearGradient())), a grob as the clip (clipping path) and mask of a viewport. Cairo-based devices and pdf() only. Graphics engine version 14.

R 4.2.0

grid.group(), grid.define(), grid.use() (groups, compositing operators, affine transformations), grid.stroke(), grid.fill(), grid.fillStroke(), as.path(), as.mask(), vectors of pattern fills, and dev.capabilities(). Engine version 15.

R 4.3.0

grid.glyph() and glyphInfo(); the "clear" and "source" compositing operators redefined; quartz() supports the new features. Engine version 16. According to the lattice help page, the new default colours of lattice 0.21 are used from this release.

R 4.5.0

glyphInfo() gains rot.

R 4.6.0

glyphFont() gains variations (engine version 17); convertWidth() and friends convert to "snpc".

lattice 0.20

Uses dev.hold() and dev.flush() for smoother drawing; parallel() deprecated for parallelplot(); scales = list(equispaced.log = FALSE).

lattice 0.21

New default colour scheme (classic.theme("pdf") restores the old one); the smooth argument of panel.xyplot(); auto.key improvements and auto.key and grid settable in lattice.options(); the "grid" vignette; a corrected call component in trellis objects.

lattice 0.22

"data.frame" methods for all high-level functions; larrows(), lpolygon(), lrect() and lsegments() are generic; paths with holes in lpolypath(); parallel() defunct.

Source: lattice package documentation: NEWS

The NEWS for R 4.6.1 lists no change to grid or lattice. The R-devel NEWS (the upcoming 4.7.0, labelled as such and never run here) lists only bug fixes in grid: "null" widths and heights of a layout are zero when there is no space to allocate, a crash in gpar() with a very long fontfamily is fixed, cairo_pdf() no longer ignores grid.newpage() after a glyph grob in a masked viewport, and grid.pack() with row.after, row.before, col.after and col.before is fixed. Behaviour described on this page is that of R 4.6.1.

Where older tutorials differ

Older tutorial writes Current practice Why Since

xyplot(y ~ x) in a function or loop and expects a plot

print(xyplot(y ~ x)) or return the object and print at top level

The print method draws; automatic printing is off in functions and loops (R FAQ 7.22)

always

xyplot(y ~ x, type = c("p", "r", "g"))

xyplot(y ~ x, smooth = "lm", grid = TRUE)

smooth and grid are the documented preferred forms; type is kept for compatibility

lattice 0.21 (smooth), 0.19 (grid)

trellis.device("postscript", color = FALSE) and trellis.par.set(theme = col.whitebg()) at the top of a script

Open any device; use the defaults, or par.settings = for one plot

The default theme is device-independent and, since R 4.3.0, based on modern palettes

R 4.3.0

Blue and magenta symbols as the default look

The HCL/Okabe-Ito look; classic.theme("pdf") for the old one

New defaults in lattice 0.21

R 4.3.0

panel = function(x, y) { panel.xyplot(x, y); lines(lowess(x, y)) }

panel = function(x, y, ...) { panel.xyplot(x, y, ...); panel.loess(x, y) }

Grid-based panel functions, and ... to receive the call’s other arguments

always

par(mfrow = c(2, 2)) before lattice calls

print(p, split = c(col, row, 2, 2))

always

always

lattice 0.22

push.viewport(), pop.viewport(), grid.convertX(), grid.collection(), convertNative()

pushViewport(), popViewport(), convertX(), gTree(), convertUnit()

The old names are defunct and raise an error that names the replacement

—

grid.prompt(TRUE)

devAskNewPage(TRUE)

grid.prompt() was removed

R 3.0.0

Reaching into a unit’s list structure (unclass(u)[[1]])

as.numeric(u), unitType(u), convertUnit()

The internal representation of units changed

R 4.0.0

dev.new(), x11() to open a window in a script

A file device (png(), pdf(), svg()) with dev.off()

A script has no screen; the default device writes Rplots.pdf

always

attach(df) before xyplot(y ~ x)

xyplot(y ~ x, data = df)

data is searched first and does not depend on the search path

always
